source: Sun, Hu, Zhou, Zheng, Hajishirzi, Dziri, Song (2025) OMEGA: Can LLMs Reason Outside the Box in Math? Exploratory, Compositional, Transformative Generalization
finding: First benchmark that maps Boden's three types onto train/test splits. Transformative items need the model to drop a familiar tactic for a new one. Frontier models fall to zero as complexity rises. RL on Qwen helps exploratory items, barely helps compositional ones, and does almost nothing on transformative ones.
numbers: Frontier models tested: DeepSeek-R1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, o3-mini, o4-mini, 100 samples per complexity level. 40 template generators, 6 math domains, 7 transformative settings. After RL on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, transformative OOD accuracy stays near 0% in most settings; only setting 7 gained +10 pp, and only on simple variants where the old tactic still worked. Compositional gains of +7.5 pp and +15 pp in the best settings.
quote: RL consistently boosts performance on in-distribution tasks, however, accuracy on OOD problems remains near zero across most settings
limits: Math only; programmatic templates; small Qwen fine-tuning, not frontier training. 'Transformative' is defined by the authors as a tactic switch, a narrow reading of Boden.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct test of O4/O8-type moves. More prompting or RL inside the same space did not produce a rule change. The agent needs an explicit step that names the failing tactic and swaps it.

source: Suzuki, Banaei-Kashani (2026) Universe of Thoughts: A Computational Framework for Creative Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Turns Boden's three modes into three LLM search programs. T-UoT first splits a problem into mutable rules and immutable requirements, then proposes edits (remove, relax, invert, add, replace), gates each edit, then searches under the new rules. This is the closest published match to a transformational operator inside an LLM loop.
numbers: Gate keeps an edit only if it keeps the goal, keeps the core difficulty and opens a new region (soft thresholds default 2). GPT-4o, 10 generations per method and task: T-UoT human-rated Creativity 0.680 on Bridge and 0.620 on Electricity (best of matched methods); LLM-rated 0.698 and 0.526. Ablation on 100 HypoArena tasks: full T-UoT preferred over no-transformation in 54.2% of comparisons (C-UoT: 58.3%).
quote: transformational reasoning modifies the rules or constraints that define that space
limits: New self-built tasks; judges are LLMs plus a human check; the 54.2% margin is small. Scores are relative, not absolute.
agent_relevance: Template for an O4/O6 operator: extract rules, edit one, gate it, re-solve under the edit. The gate by goal-preservation is code-checkable.

source: Suzuki, Banaei-Kashani (2026) Universe of Thoughts, HypoArena results on Qwen3-14B and GLM-4-9B
finding: On hypothesis generation, transformation is not the winner. Exploratory search wins on Qwen3-14B. Transformation ranks near the bottom on average but wins single tasks. The winner changes with the backbone model.
numbers: Qwen3-14B, 100 tasks (34 bio, 34 ML, 32 social): E-UoT first with 32.7% pairwise win rate, next best 25.5%. Ranking: E-UoT, ToT, EGoT, CoT, C-UoT, T-UoT, OnePrompt. T-UoT top-ranked on 11 of 100 tasks (6 uniquely). On GLM-4-9B the plain one-prompt method ranks first (46.3% win rate). Cost: T-UoT and C-UoT cost 27.6x to 52.5x one prompt, yet scored below E-UoT at 10x.
limits: Judge is Gemma-3-12B (other judges checked). Small backbones. Token cost confounds.
agent_relevance: Do not make rule change a default. It pays on some tasks and costs 30x to 50x tokens. Fire it only on a signal (G1). Search structure beat token count.

source: Suzuki, Banaei-Kashani (2026) Universe of Thoughts, failure analysis
finding: The bottleneck for rule-changing is not finding a good new rule. The model finds reasonable rule edits but then does not carry their consequences into the final answer. Forcing it to write out the mechanism that follows from the new rule fixes much of this.
numbers: Of the 12 largest applied-transform failures, 7 had reasonable transformations not turned into competitive hypotheses; 5 were weak or misaimed. Forcing a derived mechanistic consequence raised average rank from #7 to #2.5 on frozen failure cases. Preserving the analogy mapping for C-UoT raised rank from #4 to #1.5.
limits: Frozen failure cases only; intervention is diagnostic, not a full repair; four seeds.
agent_relevance: After O4 changes a rule, add a mandatory step: derive what the new rule implies, then solve. Code can check the step exists.

source: Franceschelli, Musolesi (2024) On the Creativity of Large Language Models
finding: Argues that current LLMs can reach combinational and perhaps exploratory creativity but not transformational creativity, because they follow the training distribution and RLHF/DPO makes outputs less diverse. Says new learning architectures are probably needed.
numbers: No experiments. Position paper in AI & Society. Uses Boden's value, novelty and surprise.
quote: Transformational creativity is not achievable through the current LLM training solutions.
limits: Argument, not measurement. Predates reasoning models and agent loops. Later work (OMEGA, UoT) tests the claim only in narrow settings.
agent_relevance: Sets the prior: expect no spontaneous rule change from a plain model. Any rule change has to be forced by the scaffold.

source: Ismayilzada, Paul, Bosselut, van der Plas (2024) Creativity in AI: Progresses and Challenges
finding: Survey of AI creativity. Describes Boden's three types as combinatorial, exploratory (open-ended search of a conceptual space) and transformational (fundamental change of the space, example non-Euclidean geometry). Finds models weak at creative problem solving, abstraction and compositionality, with low diversity and originality.
numbers: Survey, no new numbers. Four areas: creative problem solving, linguistic, artistic, scientific.
limits: Treats transformational creativity in a few lines; no tests of it. Calls for process-based evaluation.
agent_relevance: Confirms the field has almost no direct measurement of transformational moves in LLMs; our own test would be new data.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
finding: RL with verifiable rewards raises pass@1 but base models win at large k. Every reasoning path of the RL model is already in the base model's samples. In Boden's terms RL sharpens exploration of the existing space and does not change it. Distillation from a stronger teacher did widen the boundary.
numbers: Pass@1 on the training set rose from 26.1 to 42.5 while pass@256 fell as RL progressed. Raising rollouts from 8 to 32, or raising temperature, did not close the gap. Manual CoT check on the hardest GSM8K items: base 24 of 25 had a valid CoT, RL 23 of 25. Qwen2.5 7B/14B/32B and LLaMA-3.1-8B, six RLVR algorithms.
quote: all reasoning paths in the RLVR model are already present in the base model
limits: Math, code, vision benchmarks; mid-size models; later training recipes may differ. Authors left large-scale RLVR scaling open.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that the space is set by the base model. Sampling many attempts inside one frame explores; it does not transform. Only a different source (a teacher, a tool, another frame) was shown to widen it.

source: Jiang, Chai, Li, Liu, Fok, Dziri, Tsvetkov, Sap, Albalak, Choi (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: Models are trapped in a shared space. 25 models answering open-ended prompts fall into the same few clusters, so more samples or more models do not give new frames.
numbers: INFINITY-CHAT: 26K real open-ended queries, 31,250 human annotations (25 raters per item), 70+ models studied. Same-model repeats with min-p decoding: 81% of pairs above 0.7 similarity, 61.2% above 0.8. Cross-model average similarity 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82). Paraphrased prompts: 0.781 similarity vs 0.821 for the original.
limits: Embedding similarity is a proxy; English prompts from WildChat; a snapshot of 2025 models.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant to G4: samples and voters from one model, or from different models, share one conceptual space, so ensembling cannot replace a rule change.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review: LLM ideas rated more novel than expert ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility. But the generator hits a diversity ceiling: most generated ideas are duplicates.
numbers: Novelty (1-10): human 4.84 (SD 1.79), AI 5.64 (SD 1.76), AI + human rerank 5.81 (SD 1.66), p<0.01 in Test 1. Of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 were non-duplicate (cosine above 0.8 counts as duplicate), about 5%. LLM self-evaluation judged unreliable.
limits: Ideas only, not executed projects; novelty is reviewer opinion. Authors flag this and propose an execution study.
agent_relevance: Ideas rated novel are cheap; new frames are not. Over-generate then rank hits a duplicate wall at about 5% unique.

source: Chakrabarty, Laban, Agarwal, Muresan, Wu (2024) Art or Artifice? Large Language Models and the False Promise of Creativity
finding: Used the Torrance Test for Creative Writing (14 tests) on stories. Expert stories passed far more tests than LLM stories, and LLMs could not reproduce expert judgments of creativity.
numbers: New Yorker stories pass on average 84.7% of 14 tests (11.9 of 14). LLM stories are 3 to 10 times less likely to pass an individual test. ChatGPT and Claude stories pass about 9% to 30%.
limits: Short stories, 2023 models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude v1.3); small expert N; measures originality in form and structure, not rule change directly.
agent_relevance: LLM judges cannot grade creativity (supports G5). A rule-change step needs a code-side check, not a model judge.

source: Lu, Sclar, Hallinan et al. (2025) AI as Humanity's Salieri: Quantifying Linguistic Creativity of Language Models via Systematic Attribution of Machine Text against Web Text
finding: CREATIVITY INDEX measures how much of a text can be rebuilt from web snippets. Human professional writers score higher than LLMs, and alignment lowers it.
numbers: Professional human authors 66.2% higher CREATIVITY INDEX than LLMs on average. Alignment (RLHF) lowers LLM score by 30.1% on average. As a zero-shot machine-text detector it beat DetectGPT by 30.2%.
limits: Measures rarity of wording, not whether a space was changed; web corpus coverage limits it.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap, code-computable novelty proxy against a reference corpus. It captures output rarity only, not transformation.

source: Mohammadi (2024) Creativity Has Left the Chat: The Price of Debiasing Language Models
finding: RLHF-aligned Llama-2 outputs are less diverse than the base model, cluster semantically, and return to their own attractor state when pushed away.
numbers: Three experiments: marketing personas, a Grace Hopper fact restated many ways, perturbed generation. Aligned model clusters in embedding space and has higher cosine similarity than base. No effect-size table in the text I read.
limits: One model family (Llama-2), one alignment recipe; creativity defined as syntactic and semantic diversity only.
agent_relevance: An aligned model pulls back to its own mode. A frame change in one prompt may fade within a few tokens, so a new rule should be restated by code in every later prompt.

source: Tian, Ravichander, Qin, Le Bras, Marjieh, Peng, Choi, Hope, Clark (2024) MacGyver: Are LLMs Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: 1,683 problems that force a tool to be used unlike its usual use (a break from its normal function). GPT-4 fails by proposing physically infeasible actions. Self-reflection helped GPT-4 only; divergent-convergent prompting helped all models tried.
numbers: 323-problem sample for human comparison. Majority of humans correct 79.3% vs GPT-4 73.3%. Error types in 200 failed GPT-4 solutions: wrong tool use 42.4%, goal not achieved 17.7%, unavailable tools 16.9%, unfaithful to constraints 9.5%. 78% solvable, 22% unsolvable; GPT-4 seldom flags an unsolvable problem. Llama2 self-reflection did not reduce infeasible answers (it called its first answer wrong every time).
limits: Physical-reasoning domain; 2023 models (PaLM2, Claude2, Llama2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4); per-prompt effect sizes only in figures.
agent_relevance: Functional-fixedness break is a small-scale rule change (what a tool is for). Divergent-then-convergent beat blind reflection; reflection alone backfires on weak models (G1, G2).

source: Pan, Xie, Wilson (2025) Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively
finding: Little Alchemy 2 as an open-ended discovery task. Most LLMs find fewer new elements than humans. Only o1 beats humans. Models lean on uncertainty and use empowerment late; prompt tricks did not help.
numbers: 29,493 humans, 4,691,033 trials. Elements found in 500 trials: LLaMA3.1-8B 9, LLaMA3.1-70B 25, GPT-4o 35, DeepSeek-R1 85, o1 177, humans 42 (51 over all trials). GPT-4o with CoT, self-reflection and explicit strategy hints: average 43, t = -1.17, p = 0.304 (no gain).
limits: One game, 720 elements, deterministic rules; sparse-autoencoder analysis on open models only.
agent_relevance: Exploration depth came from longer iterative reasoning, not from instructions. A program-kept record of tried combinations is the alternative to asking for more exploration.

source: Hu, Lu, Clune (2025) Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS)
finding: A meta agent writes new agent code into a growing archive, so the agent design space itself is searched. This is a rule-space search, an operational form of transformation over agent designs.
numbers: Discovered agents beat hand-designed baselines: DROP F1 +13.6/100, MGSM accuracy +14.4%, and when transferred GSM8K +25.9% and GSM-Hard +13.2%.
limits: Gains on benchmarks with a scoring signal; the design space is code, so changes are limited to what the meta agent can express.
agent_relevance: Transformation worked when a verifiable score gated each change. Suggests O4/O6 should accept rule changes only if they pass a held-out check (G3).

source: Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune (2026) Darwin Godel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents
finding: A coding agent rewrites its own code and keeps an archive of all variants (open-ended). Without self-improvement, or without the open-ended archive, results are lower.
numbers: SWE-bench 20.0% to 50.0%; Polyglot 14.2% to 30.7% on the full benchmark (14.0% to 38.0% on the 50-task subset). Best SWE-bench agent scores 28.9% on Polyglot when transferred. Ablations: DGM w/o self-improve and DGM w/o open-ended exploration both lower. 80 iterations.
limits: Coding benchmarks with objective tests; costly; needs sandbox.
agent_relevance: Keeping poor intermediate variants in an archive lets later changes build on a stepping stone. A single-path loop loses this.

source: Faldor, Zhang, Cully, Clune (2025) OMNI-EPIC: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness with Environments Programmed in Code
finding: An LLM proposes the next task and writes its environment and reward code, filtered by a model of interestingness and an archive. It removes the hand-set limit of the task distribution, a form of space widening.
numbers: Compared with two controls (no archive; no interestingness model): higher task cell coverage (3 simulated runs, p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U) and higher ANNECS-OMNI (5 RL runs, p<0.05).
limits: Interestingness is judged by an LLM; authors admit environments may resemble training data; simulator limits it.
agent_relevance: Novelty needs both an archive of what exists and a filter for worth. Same two parts as our guardrails.

source: Schapiro, Black, Varshney (2025) Transformational Creativity in Science: A Graphical Theory
finding: Models a scientific space as a graph where axioms are nodes that rules depend on. Proves that changing an axiom has the most transformative potential, and fits historical cases (e.g. non-Euclidean geometry) to it.
numbers: Formal proof plus case illustrations; no experiments.
limits: No empirical test; the graph model is the authors' own. Short paper.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule for choosing what to alter: change the item with most dependents (an axiom), not a leaf. A dependency graph of assumptions could be built and ranked by code.

source: Liapis, Martinez, Togelius, Yannakakis (2013; arXiv 2021) Transforming Exploratory Creativity with DeLeNoX
finding: Older AI system. Alternates novelty-search exploration with an autoencoder that relearns the distance measure, so the criteria of the next search change. Authors treat the exploratory-transformational line as a matter of degree.
numbers: Spaceship sprites 49x49 pixels; 6 iterations; 1000 spaceships per training set; denoising autoencoder with 64 hidden features, 1000 epochs. A transforming run was compared with a static run that kept the initial features. The static run's ships were simpler than the transforming run's at the same CPPN size.
limits: Case study, one domain; no human ratings; results shown in figures, not tables.
agent_relevance: Change the measure of novelty from the archive itself when exploration plateaus. A plateau is a signal (G1).

source: Espirito Santo, Wiggins, Cardoso (2024) Towards a Formal Creativity Theory: Preliminary results in Novelty and Transformativeness
finding: Uses formal learning theory to define novelty and transformational creativity as shifts of the hypothesis space under new data. Argues that novelty alone is not transformation.
numbers: Formal definitions and proofs; anecdote of 'grey music'. No experiments.
limits: Theory only.
agent_relevance: Separates 'new answer' from 'new hypothesis space'. A test for our agent: did the set of admissible answers change, or only the chosen answer?

source: Boden (2004) The Creative Mind; Wiggins (2006); Ritchie (2006) as cited in opened sources
finding: Boden: transformational creativity alters or drops a defining dimension of the conceptual space. Wiggins formalises it as exploratory search at the meta-level over the rules of the space. Seen only as citations inside sources I opened.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Not opened. Quoted via UoT, Schapiro et al. and Ismayilzada et al.
agent_relevance: Defines the target: a meta-level search over rules, with the object-level search left alone.

source: Lenat's AM and EURISKO; Cohen's AARON; Langley's BACON (older systems named in the Boden literature)
finding: Early machine systems cited as tests of rule change: EURISKO changed its own heuristics, BACON rediscovered laws. Not opened this session; named only from background knowledge.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: EURISKO is the earliest self-rule-change loop; the usual lesson drawn is that it needed hand tuning by its author.

source: Magrin-Chagnolleau (2026) Can an AI System Be Creative? A Critical Perspective from Art and Engineering
finding: Appeared in an arXiv listing for transformational creativity. Title and listing only; not read.
numbers: None.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Possible further reading for the human-factors angle.

source: Bhushan, Zhang, Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks (seen in a sibling agent's file, not opened by me)
finding: Sibling evidence file b01 reports a rubric that scores agent steps on Boden's modes (0 Routine to 4 Transformational). I read only the first line of that file. Verify before use.
numbers: Per sibling file: 3 annotators, 300 episodes, Krippendorff alpha 0.724; GPT-5 judge vs humans Spearman 0.732.
limits: Not opened by me; second-hand.
agent_relevance: If real, a rubric for labelling when an agent step changes the representation or task definition.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind, open-endedness check
finding: Even prompts rated highly open-ended did not get more varied answers across 42 models. Open-endedness of the question does not widen the space the model uses.
numbers: Average pairwise similarity: high open-endedness prompts 0.800, low open-endedness prompts 0.837 (42 models).
limits: Gap is small (0.037); classification of open-endedness was automatic.
agent_relevance: Asking 'be creative' or posing a wide question is not a rule change. Do not count it as one.

source: Pan, Xie, Wilson (2025) Little Alchemy 2, reasoning-model trace analysis
finding: DeepSeek-R1 shows repeated cycles of combination analysis and past-trial analysis, close to human-like exploration, but tries more failed combinations than o1 and humans do. Sparse-autoencoder analysis puts uncertainty and choice earlier in the network and empowerment later, so fast models decide before empowerment is computed.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 found 85 elements vs o1 177 vs humans 42 in 500 trials. Prompt engineering on GPT-4o gave no significant gain (mean 43, p = 0.304).
limits: Mechanism claim from SAE analysis on open models; correlational.
agent_relevance: Time to think and a record of past trials, not instruction, changed discovery counts. Supports a code-kept history of tried frames.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver, prompting interventions
finding: Two prompts tested: iterative step-wise reflection (check each step is physically possible, then edit) and divergent-convergent thinking (generate many, then select). Reflection helped GPT-4 but not Llama2 models; divergent-convergent helped every model tried.
numbers: Size of gains is shown only in figures. Reflection on Llama2 always claimed the first answer was wrong and changed it blindly.
limits: Figures only; 2023 models; one domain.
agent_relevance: Revision needs a real failing signal (G2). Blind 'reflect' on a weak model made answers worse or unchanged.
